section.title: Praise for Deliverance
section.sectionRationale: Within the Isaiah apocalypse, chapters 24 to 27, this chapter answers the devastation of chapter 24 with a song of praise. The prophet turns from describing a shattered earth to worship, and the LORD's plan reaches its high point: a banquet on Mount Zion for all peoples and the swallowing up of death itself, a promise later quoted in 1 Corinthians 15:54 of the resurrection.
section.thesis: The LORD who humbled ruthless cities becomes a refuge for the poor and needy, and on His mountain He prepares a feast for all peoples while swallowing up death forever, wiping every tear away, so that His waiting people can say at last, this is our God, we have waited for Him.
section.frameNote: Five movements: praise for the LORD's faithful wonders and the ruined fortress of strangers; the LORD as refuge and stronghold for the poor; the banquet on the mountain and the swallowing up of death; the joyful confession, this is our God; and the LORD's hand resting on Zion while pride is brought low.

units.label: Praise for the LORD's faithful wonders

verses.text: O LORD, You are my God! I will exalt You; I will praise Your name. For You have worked wonders, plans formed long ago, in perfect faithfulness.
Indeed, You have made the city a heap of rubble, the fortified town a ruin. The fortress of strangers is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt.
Therefore, a strong people will honor You. The cities of ruthless nations will revere You.

units.label: A refuge for the poor and needy
units.note: shade from the heat, shelter from the storm

verses.text: For You have been a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress, a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat. For the breath of the ruthless is like rain against a wall,
like heat in a dry land. You subdue the uproar of foreigners. As the shade of a cloud cools the heat, so the song of the ruthless is silenced.

units.label: A banquet on the mountain, death swallowed up

verses.text: On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a {{mishteh|banquet}} for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat, of finely aged wine.
On this mountain He will {{bala|swallow up}} the shroud that enfolds all peoples, the sheet that covers all nations;
He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth. For the LORD has spoken.

units.label: This is our God, we have waited for Him

verses.text: And in that day it will be said, “Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us. This is the LORD for whom we have waited. Let us rejoice and be glad in His salvation.”

units.label: The LORD's hand rests on Zion, pride brought low
units.note: Moab as an example of humbled pride

verses.text: For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain. But Moab will be trampled in his place as straw is trodden into the dung pile.
He will spread out his hands within it, as a swimmer spreads his arms to swim. His pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands.
The high-walled fortress will be brought down, cast to the ground, into the dust.

mishteh.gloss: A feast or banquet, often marking celebration, covenant, or royal favor. The LORD's banquet here is for all peoples, not Israel alone, a rich foreshadowing of the messianic banquet and the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9.

bala.gloss: To swallow up, devour, or engulf completely. Used twice in quick succession, first of the shroud of mourning over all peoples and then, climactically, of death itself, a word Paul quotes directly in 1 Corinthians 15:54 to describe Christ's resurrection victory.

basic.context: After the devastation of chapter 24, Isaiah bursts into personal praise, celebrating that the LORD has ruined a proud, oppressive fortress and become instead a refuge for the poor and needy. The chapter reaches its high point in a breathtaking promise: on His mountain, the LORD will host a banquet for all peoples and swallow up death itself forever, wiping every tear from every face.
basic.hermeneutics: The ruined city and fortress likely reflect a real historical humbling of an oppressive power, while the banquet and the swallowing up of death, verses 6 to 8, reach beyond any single historical event toward God's final, universal salvation. Paul's use of verse 8 in 1 Corinthians 15:54 confirms that its ultimate fulfillment is the bodily resurrection secured in Christ, even as its first hearers likely heard a nearer hope of rescue as well.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD will bala, swallow up, first the shroud of mourning covering the nations and then death itself, the very word Paul quotes when celebrating Christ's resurrection victory, 1 Corinthians 15:54. This same mountain hosts a mishteh, banquet, for all peoples, not Israel alone, hinting at a salvation with a scope as wide as the death it overturns.
basic.typology: The banquet the LORD prepares on His mountain for all peoples anticipates the messianic feast Jesus repeatedly pictures in His parables and the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The swallowing up of death and the wiping away of every tear anticipate the new creation described in Revelation 21:4, both drawing directly on this chapter's language.
basic.christ: Paul explicitly quotes verse 8, death is swallowed up in victory, in 1 Corinthians 15:54, tying this ancient promise directly to Christ's bodily resurrection and the future resurrection of all who trust in Him. The banquet for all peoples anticipates the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the wiping away of every tear is picked up nearly word for word in Revelation 21:4, showing that Christ personally accomplishes what this chapter promises.
basic.god: God is a refuge for the poor and needy precisely because He first humbles ruthless, oppressive power; His strength serves the weak rather than crushing them further. His salvation reaches beyond any one nation to a banquet, a shroud lifted, and death swallowed up for all peoples, revealing a heart set on the widest possible rescue.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15:54-57 quotes Isaiah 25:8 directly as fulfilled in Christ's resurrection victory over death. Revelation 21:4 echoes wiping away every tear in the description of the new creation. Revelation 19:9 pictures the marriage supper of the Lamb, the fulfillment of this chapter's banquet for all peoples. Luke 14:15-24 records Jesus' own parable of a great banquet open to all who will come.
basic.oneStory: This chapter moves from praise for a humbled oppressor to the LORD's astonishing promise of a banquet for all peoples and the swallowing up of death itself. It is one of the Old Testament's clearest advance glimpses of the gospel, fulfilled when Christ rose from the dead and secured the resurrection hope and endless feast this chapter foresees.

context.literary:
Chapter 25 is the first answer to the devastation of chapter 24, and it is built like a hinge. Verses 1 to 5 are prayer, spoken straight to God in the second person. Verses 6 to 8 switch to prophecy in the third person, with the LORD of Hosts as the one acting. Verse 9 turns to the congregation and tells them what they will say in that day. Verses 10 to 12 return to prophecy, and the tone hardens again. The banquet therefore sits between two scenes of humbled pride, the ruined fortress at the start and Moab in the dust at the end.

Small repetitions carry the weight. 'On this mountain' opens verse 6 and verse 7 and comes back in verse 10, so that the feast, the unveiling of the nations and the resting hand of the LORD all happen in one place. The word 'ruthless' falls three times in verses 3 to 5. The ruthless are described through weather, a breath like rain against a wall, a presence like heat in a dry land, and then they are hushed as a cloud's shade cools the heat. The poor, meanwhile, are given the same weather as a mercy: a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat.

The chapter also talks to its neighbours. The city of chaos in 24:10 becomes a heap of rubble here, and the humbled lofty city returns in 26:5 and 27:10, set against the strong city of 26:1. Chapters 24 to 27 are often called the Isaiah apocalypse, and this chapter is the first of three songs in that block, followed by the song of 26:1 and the song of the vineyard in 27:2. Notice, finally, the movement of tense. Verses 1 to 5 look back at what God has done. Verse 9 looks forward, 'in that day,' and speaks as though the waiting were already over. The faith of the chapter lives in that grammar.
context.historical:
Isaiah's ministry stretched from the reign of Uzziah to the reign of Hezekiah, Isaiah 1:1, and chapters 24 to 27 do not name the occasion that prompted them. That silence is deliberate. The 'city' of verse 2 is left unnamed, a fortress of strangers that stands for every proud power that crushed the weak, so that the song can be sung over Nineveh, Babylon or any later city without losing its force. Readers have proposed particular candidates, but the text itself offers none, and the careful path is to hear the city as a type rather than a puzzle to be solved.

The images were rooted in ordinary life. Mourners in Israel covered the head and face; David went up the Mount of Olives weeping with his head covered, 2 Samuel 15:30. The shroud that 'enfolds all peoples' is that gesture made universal, a whole humanity in mourning. A feast of aged wine was the opposite of ordinary fare. Wine left to settle on its lees was a luxury, and a banquet of choice meat meant a great occasion. Covenant making was sealed at table, as when Israel's elders ate and drank in God's presence at Sinai, Exodus 24:9-11, and kings and their vassals shared meals as signs of settled peace.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea and had been Israel's neighbour and rival from the wilderness years onward. Isaiah has already spoken against it, and what he said there is about pride, Isaiah 16:6. Jeremiah repeats the charge, Jeremiah 48:29. Moab is named here as an example, probably because its pride was proverbial. Straw trodden into a dung pit was a picture of what is made worthless and useful for nothing but rot.
context.canonical:
Earlier Scripture prepares for nearly every image. A meal in God's presence appears at Sinai, where the elders 'saw Him, and they ate and drank,' Exodus 24:11, and in the shepherd's table prepared 'in the presence of my enemies' in Psalm 23:5. Wisdom sets a table and sends out her maidservants with an invitation, Proverbs 9:1-5. The mountain that draws all nations is already in view in Isaiah 2:2-3, and the free feast for the thirsty comes again in Isaiah 55:1-2. Death as an enemy goes back to Genesis 2:17 and 3:19, and a nearby prophet makes the same promise of ransom from the grave, Hosea 13:14.

Later Scripture takes up the chapter again and again. Jesus told of a great banquet and said that many would come from east and west to the feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Matthew 8:11. At the last supper He spoke of drinking the cup anew in His Father's kingdom, Matthew 26:29. Paul quotes verse 8 at the climax of his argument about resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:54. Paul also tells Timothy that Christ 'has abolished death,' 2 Timothy 1:10. John twice borrows the tear-wiping line, Revelation 7:17 and 21:4, and sets the marriage supper of the Lamb in Revelation 19:9.

So the chapter works as a hinge in the whole Bible's hope. It collects what Sinai and the Psalms hinted at, extends it from one nation to all peoples, and hands it to the apostles as the shape of the end.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted his hearers to learn how to look at the cities of the world. Empires rise with walls and ruthless confidence, and to a small nation living under their shadow they seemed permanent. The prophet teaches Judah to see them as provisional and to see something else as permanent: a God whose plans were laid long ago and who keeps faith with the weak. The opening prayer is personal on purpose. It models a believer who has seen the pattern and answers it with worship, 'You are my God,' before the rescue has fully arrived.

He also meant them to be startled. The feast is for 'all the peoples,' and the shroud covers all nations. A people used to thinking of Gentile powers as enemies are told that the God of Zion intends a table for their oppressors' subjects too. At the same time the Moab scene warns Israel that pride has no exemption. The hand that rests on the mountain for blessing is the same hand that presses pride into the dust.

Above all he meant them to wait well. Verse 9 puts words in their mouths, 'we have waited for Him, and He has saved us,' and the structure implies that waiting is not an idle interval but part of the faith itself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what God will do and how His people will answer. It does not give a programme for building the banquet or for dealing with Moab. There is no command to overthrow a fortress, and no instruction to gloat. The people sing, they wait, and they see what God does. Those who read the final verses as permission to celebrate the ruin of a neighbouring people mistake a prophecy of divine judgment for a mandate for human triumph. Scripture itself forbids that spirit, Proverbs 24:17, and Moab's daughter Ruth sits in the line of David, Ruth 4:17.

What does carry forward is the shape of faithful life under pressure. Believers are meant to praise before the outcome, to treat the care of the poor and needy as the way God Himself acts, and to hold the promise of verse 8 as a settled fact that steadies grief now. The text also gives comfort a form: not a denial of tears but a promise that God will wipe them away.

debates.question: How much of the banquet and the swallowing up of death, verses 6 to 8, was understood or fulfilled in Isaiah's own time, and how much awaits final consummation?

views.label: Primarily an eschatological promise, understood only in shadow by its first hearers
views.case: The scope, all peoples, and the totality of the promise, death swallowed up forever, exceed any plausible near historical fulfillment, suggesting the original audience grasped only a partial hope that the New Testament later unveils fully in Christ.

views.label: A promise with a real, if partial, near fulfillment alongside its ultimate horizon
views.case: Prophetic literature often layers a near, historical rescue, here perhaps deliverance from a specific oppressor, together with a further, final fulfillment, meaning the first hearers could have experienced genuine relief that also functioned as a partial down payment on the fuller promise.

debates.bearing: However one weighs the near and far horizons, the New Testament's direct citation of verse 8 regarding the resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:54, settles that its ultimate and complete fulfillment is found in Christ, whatever partial comfort earlier believers may have also drawn from it.

debates.question: Does 'all the peoples' mean that every person will be saved, or people drawn from every nation?

views.label: Every person without exception
views.case: The language is sweeping. The feast is for all the peoples, the shroud covers all nations, and the disgrace of God's people is removed from the whole earth. Some read the promise at face value as God's intention to restore everyone, and they point to the swallowing up of death forever as leaving no one behind.

views.label: People from every nation, with real judgment alongside
views.case: The same chapter that spreads the feast speaks of the ruthless silenced and Moab trampled, verses 5 and 10 to 12, and verse 9 describes a people who say 'we have waited for Him.' Prophets elsewhere gather survivors from the nations, Isaiah 66:19-21, and John sees a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9, which is a company drawn out of the nations, not a count of every individual.

debates.bearing: The chapter itself holds both a wide welcome and a firm refusal of pride, and the New Testament keeps that tension, with a worldwide invitation and a real division, John 5:28-29. The safest reading takes the breadth of the invitation as sincere and the closing scene as a warning that the table is received by trust, not by birth or by power.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 calls God's acts 'wonders,' from the Hebrew pele. The word is reserved for deeds that go beyond what any human power could do, and Israel first sang it at the sea, where God was 'working wonders,' Exodus 15:11. It sits inside the name given to the coming king, 'Wonderful Counselor,' Isaiah 9:6. The 'plans formed long ago' in the same verse are God's counsels, and the closing phrase, 'in perfect faithfulness,' stacks two words from the same family, emunah and omen, a doubled certainty. Isaiah 28:29 will bring the same pair, wonder and counsel, back at the close of chapter 28, and Isaiah 46:10 says why the plans can be trusted: God declares the end from the beginning.

In verse 4 God is a 'refuge' and a 'stronghold,' and the Hebrew uses two different nouns. The first is machseh, a shelter you run into for cover, and the second is maoz, a fortified place that holds against attack. The poor receive both: cover from the storm and walls against the enemy. The 'fortress' of strangers in verse 2, by contrast, is a human stronghold that will not be rebuilt. The chapter measures two kinds of security against each other.

The 'aged wine' of verse 6 comes from shemarim, a word tied to the lees or dregs on which wine was left to settle. Wine rested on its lees became rich and clear once strained, and so the phrase means wine at its finest, kept for a day of celebration. The repetition in the verse, aged wine twice, adds emphasis.

In verse 8 the 'disgrace' of His people is cherpah, reproach, the taunt that foreign powers threw at a defeated Israel. It is the word for what the seven women in Isaiah 4:1 want to be rid of. God removes not only the sorrow but the public shame.

The waiting of verse 9 uses qavah, to wait with tension, a verb often linked with the noun for a cord pulled taut. It is the verb of Isaiah 40:31, where those who 'wait upon the LORD' renew their strength. The verb of salvation in the same verse shares its root with the name Jesus, yeshua, which in Hebrew means salvation.

Finally, verse 8 'swallow up' leaves the question of what 'forever' means. The Hebrew word behind it is lanetsach, which can mean 'for all time' and, in the Greek of Paul's day, was often rendered 'to victory.' That is why Paul writes 'swallowed up in victory' in 1 Corinthians 15:54, and the BSB footnote on Isaiah 25:8 gives both readings. The verb itself is the one used when the earth opens its mouth and swallows Korah's rebels, Numbers 16:30, and when the earth swallows Pharaoh's army, Exodus 15:12. Death, which swallows its victims, Proverbs 1:12, is finally swallowed itself.

typology.type: The feast on the mountain, from the covenant meal at Sinai
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai Israel's leaders ate and drank in God's presence and were not harmed, Exodus 24:11, a covenant meal that anticipated fellowship with Him. Isaiah widens it to all peoples. Jesus sits at the table, takes the cup and speaks of drinking it anew in His Father's kingdom, Matthew 26:29, and promises that His followers will 'eat and drink at My table in My kingdom,' Luke 22:30. John sees the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The type falls short because Sinai's meal was for seventy elders and lasted a day, while the final feast gathers a multitude that no one can number and does not end.

typology.type: Death swallowed, after the earth that swallowed Korah
typology.fulfillment: The same verb that describes the earth opening its mouth to swallow rebels, Numbers 16:30, is used of death itself being swallowed. Hosea promised ransom from Sheol, Hosea 13:14, and Paul quotes both prophets when he sees the resurrection coming, 1 Corinthians 15:54-55. Christ 'has abolished death,' 2 Timothy 1:10, by dying and rising. The picture is fulfilled in its first stage and still open in its last, because 'the last enemy to be destroyed is death,' 1 Corinthians 15:26, and Death and Hades are only thrown into the lake of fire at the end, Revelation 20:14.

typology.type: The refuge for the poor and needy, shade from the heat
typology.fulfillment: God is the refuge from storm and shade from heat, and Isaiah 32:2 says a coming king and his officers will themselves be 'a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm.' Jesus gathers the weary and the burdened and offers rest, Matthew 11:28, and when John asks if He is the one, Jesus points to the poor who have good news preached to them, Luke 7:22. The shelter from judgment is the man who stood in the storm for others, so the type is fulfilled at a cost that Isaiah does not yet show. It falls short for now because storms still break on believers until the day of verse 8.

typology.type: The shroud and the tears, Lazarus at Bethany
typology.fulfillment: At the grave of Lazarus Jesus wept, John 11:35, and then called the dead man out, with his face still wrapped in a cloth, John 11:43-44. The scene is a small acted preview of verses 7 and 8, the tears answered and the covering removed from the face. The correspondence is real but partial. Lazarus died again, while the promise of Isaiah is death swallowed up forever, as guaranteed by Christ's own resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the apostle's use of verse 8. Paul does not merely borrow a phrase. He places Isaiah's promise at the end of the resurrection argument and says it 'will come to pass' when the perishable puts on the imperishable, 1 Corinthians 15:54. The promise is therefore tied to a person, because Christ has been raised as 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the harvest will follow him. Isaiah says the LORD will swallow up death; the New Testament says it is done through the death and rising of the Son, 2 Timothy 1:10 and Hebrews 2:14-15. The tears wiped away are first seen on the face of Jesus Himself, who wept at a grave, John 11:35.

It leads to Christ through the table. The LORD of Hosts prepares the banquet, and Jesus shows Himself as the host who turns water into wine and is told 'you have saved the fine wine until now,' John 2:10. He feeds multitudes on a hillside, promises His followers a place at His table, Luke 22:29-30, and gives the cup with a promise that looks past the cross to the kingdom, Matthew 26:29. Hebrews places believers already at the heavenly Mount Zion, Hebrews 12:22. Care is needed not to turn every detail into a code, such as the aged wine becoming something specific. The links stand because the New Testament itself builds on the chapter's main images.

It leads to Christ through the removal of disgrace. The reproach that fell on God's people was borne by Jesus 'outside the city gate,' and believers are told to go to Him there 'bearing the disgrace He bore,' Hebrews 13:12-13. His shame becomes the end of theirs. The Lamb who is the shepherd leads them to living water and wipes away every tear, Revelation 7:17.

And it leads to Christ through the breadth of the guest list. A feast for all peoples runs from Isaiah to the Great Commission and to the song of the redeemed from every tribe and tongue, Revelation 5:9. The One who makes room at the table is the One who was slain, and the invitation of Isaiah 25 remains the invitation of the gospel.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows is God's long faithfulness. The prayer begins with personal ownership, 'You are my God,' and then gives the reason: He has done wonders, 'plans formed long ago, in perfect faithfulness.' The ruin of the fortress is not an accident of history but a plan that He has been working for a very long time. God is not improvising in a crisis. He is keeping a purpose that was settled before the tyrants arose.

He is the God of the weak. The pairing of verse 4, a refuge for the poor and a stronghold for the needy, shows power in the service of the powerless. The same power that silences the ruthless is the cover for the oppressed, and the same strength that humbles a high-walled fortress, verse 12, lifts the needy. The doctrine of God that comes out of this is that strength and mercy are not rivals in Him but two sides of one character.

He is a God of hospitality. He prepares the table Himself, and He does it for peoples who had no claim on Him. At the same time He is the God who judges pride, as verses 10 to 12 make plain. The tension is real, and it is held together by verse 9: those who waited for Him are those who sit at the feast, and the pride that cannot wait is the pride that ends in dust.

He is tender. The mighty LORD of Hosts in verse 6 becomes the Lord GOD who wipes tears from every face in verse 8. The sovereign who swallows death is the one who handles each wet cheek with His own hand. The closing line, 'For the LORD has spoken,' sets the whole promise on His word.

For worship, the chapter gives words and a tense. The words are the opening praise and the confession of verse 9. The tense is the future spoken as present, a people who rejoice 'in His salvation' while they are still waiting. Worship here is not an after-the-fact thank you but a way of living between the promise and its arrival.

crossReferences.note: The preceding chapter ends with the LORD of Hosts reigning on Mount Zion before His elders with great glory. The mountain of chapter 25 is that mountain, and the banquet is what His reign looks like at close range, a king who makes a feast for His people and the nations.

The elders of Israel saw God and ate and drank, and He did not lay His hand on them. Isaiah's feast turns that mountaintop meal from a privilege of seventy leaders into an invitation to all peoples, and the God who once stayed His hand from the nobles now removes the shroud from every face.

Wisdom prepares her meat, mixes her wine, sets her table and sends out her maidservants to call the simple to eat and drink. The banquet is an old biblical picture of life offered by God, and Isaiah gives it its largest scale: the feast of wisdom becomes the feast at the end of the age.

God says He will ransom from the power of Sheol and redeem from Death. The promise is spoken as a challenge to Death itself. Isaiah and Hosea together are the two Old Testament texts Paul sets side by side in 1 Corinthians 15:54-55, and they show that the swallowing of death was a recurring prophetic hope.

The thirsty are invited to come to the waters and to eat without money and without cost. This is the same open table as Isaiah 25:6, seen from the invitation side. Together they show that the feast is a gift. The only thing needed is to come, and the only thing refused is the labour that does not satisfy.

A coming king and his princes will each be 'a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm.' The refuge and shade that God provides in Isaiah 25:4 are here given human form in the righteous ruler, and the pair prepare the way for a Messiah who both shelters and reigns.

Isaiah's earlier oracle names the sin of Moab as pride, pomposity, conceit and arrogance. When chapter 25 picks Moab as its closing picture, it assumes the reader remembers that charge. Moab stands for pride in general, and the sentence is the one Scripture gives to pride everywhere.

After marvelling at a Roman centurion's faith, Jesus says that many will come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The Gentile welcome that Isaiah announced begins to arrive in the ministry of Jesus, and He places Himself as the one who decides who sits at the table.

At a dinner a guest says blessed is everyone who eats at the feast in God's kingdom, and Jesus replies with a parable of a banquet whose invited guests make excuses so that the poor and the outsiders are brought in. It is a sharp reading of Isaiah's feast: the table is ready, but those who think they own the invitation can miss it.

Jesus saw Mary weeping, was deeply moved in spirit and troubled, and wept. The God who promises to wipe away tears is shown in the Gospel sharing them first. The next scene removes the shroud from a dead man's face, an early sign that Isaiah's picture has a Person standing behind it.

Paul says that Christ Jesus 'has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel.' The verb abolished is the New Testament's way of saying what Isaiah said with 'swallow up.' The defeat of death is already announced and begun in the gospel, even if its last stage waits.

The Lamb at the center of the throne becomes the shepherd who leads His people to living water, and God wipes away every tear from their eyes. John takes Isaiah's promise and sets it in the mouth of a vision of the redeemed, showing who does the wiping and where.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that Genesis leaves hanging. After Eden the story is one of death, shame and dispersal: the ground cursed, the human race sent east, Babel's proud tower scattering the peoples. Genesis 3:19 gave death its sentence, and Genesis 11 gave the nations their separation. Isaiah 25 is where the Old Testament first says plainly that God means to undo both. The shroud over all peoples is lifted, and the table that He sets gathers them again.

It also answers the cities. From Cain's first city to Babel, Genesis traces a line of human strongholds built to keep God out or to make a name. Isaiah sets the fortress of strangers against the refuge of the poor and says which one will stand. The same tension runs through the prophets and into Revelation, where Babylon falls in a single hour and the New Jerusalem comes down from God.

After Isaiah the story moves in three steps. First it narrows, as Israel is exiled and the promise looks dead. Then it opens in Christ, who dies, rises, and is declared the firstfruits of the final harvest. Paul can then quote verse 8 as something now certain. In the third step the promise runs through the church, which holds the table in the Lord's Supper while it waits for the great supper, and the mission to the nations, which is the invitation at work.

The Bible's last chapters read like a fulfilment of Isaiah's words. 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes' is the voice from the throne, and 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. God's dwelling place is with humanity, Revelation 21:3. The gathered peoples of Isaiah 25, the shroud lifted, the pride humbled and the table spread, all arrive. What began in a garden with a broken trust ends with a feast and a people who say, 'Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him.'

sermon.title: Cities of Ruthless Nations Will Revere Thee
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly through Isaiah 25:1 to 8, drawing out how the LORD's humbling of ruthless power and His becoming a refuge for the poor lead to the promise of the banquet and the swallowing up of death, the same movement this study traces to its fulfillment in Christ.

quiz.q: Why does Isaiah praise the LORD in verses 1 to 3?

options.text: Because the LORD, in perfect faithfulness, has ruined a ruthless, oppressive fortress.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 give exactly this reason for praise, God's faithful, planned action against oppression.

options.text: Because Israel has just won a major military victory on her own.
options.note: The praise is directed to the LORD's own action, not a self-achieved Israelite military victory.

options.text: Because a new temple has just been completed.
options.note: Not mentioned in this passage; the praise concerns the LORD ruining an oppressive city.

options.text: Because a famine has finally ended.
options.note: Not the stated reason here; the specific cause for praise is the humbling of a ruthless fortress.

quiz.q: What does the LORD promise to prepare on His mountain in verse 6?

options.text: A banquet, a feast of aged wine and choice meat, for all peoples.
options.note: Verse 6 explicitly describes this banquet, and specifies it is for all peoples, not Israel alone.

options.text: A courtroom trial for all the nations.
options.note: Not the image in this verse; the picture is a celebratory feast, not a trial.

options.text: A military parade celebrating conquest.
options.note: Not described here; the specific image given is a banquet.

options.text: A private feast for Israel's priests only.
options.note: The text specifically says for all peoples, not a priests-only or Israel-only banquet.

quiz.q: What astonishing promise appears in verse 8, later quoted by Paul?

options.text: He will swallow up death forever and wipe away every tear.
options.note: Verse 8 states this directly, and Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 15:54.

options.text: He will make death more frequent among the wicked.
options.note: The opposite; the promise is the total abolition of death, not its increase.

options.text: He will extend human lifespans by a few years.
options.note: Not the promise here; the text speaks of swallowing up death entirely, not merely extending life somewhat.

options.text: He will remove death only for the wealthy and powerful.
options.note: The promise applies to His people generally, removing disgrace from the whole earth, not a wealth-restricted group.

quiz.q: What is the joyful confession the people make in verse 9?

options.text: Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us.
options.note: Verse 9 gives this exact confession of long-awaited salvation.

options.text: We no longer need to trust in the LORD.
options.note: The opposite; the confession affirms continued trust and celebrates His salvation.

options.text: We built this salvation ourselves through our own strength.
options.note: The confession credits the LORD's salvation, not human achievement.

options.text: We regret having waited so long for the LORD.
options.note: The tone is joyful vindication of their waiting, not regret.

quiz.q: How does Isaiah 25:8 connect directly to the New Testament?

options.text: Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 15:54 as fulfilled in Christ's resurrection victory over death.
options.note: Paul explicitly cites this verse to celebrate the resurrection Christ has secured.

options.text: It is never referenced anywhere in the New Testament.
options.note: The opposite; it is directly and explicitly quoted by Paul.

options.text: It is quoted only in a minor, disputed manuscript variant.
options.note: It is quoted plainly and centrally in the widely accepted text of 1 Corinthians 15.

options.text: It is referenced only indirectly through vague thematic parallels.
options.note: The connection is a direct quotation, not merely an indirect thematic echo.

questions: Isaiah praises God specifically for humbling a ruthless, oppressive power and becoming a refuge for the poor. Where in your own life or community do you need to trust God as a refuge against something that feels ruthless or overwhelming?
The LORD prepares His banquet for all peoples, not one nation alone. Is there a person or group you unconsciously assume is outside the reach of God's welcome?
Death is swallowed up forever and every tear wiped away, a promise fulfilled in Christ's resurrection. What grief or fear of death are you carrying that this promise speaks directly into?

The people's confession is, we have waited for Him, and He has saved us. What are you currently waiting on God for, and how does this chapter encourage you to keep waiting in hope rather than despair?
Moab's downfall came through pride, despite the skill of his hands. Where might your own competence or self-sufficiency be quietly standing in for trust in God?

translationNotes.note: The shroud or sheet covering all peoples is a poetic image for mourning and death's universal reach, immediately answered in verse 8 by death itself being swallowed up.
Moab appears here as a specific, representative example of proud human power humbled, tying this hymn of universal hope back to the regional oracles against the nations in earlier chapters.
